case.case_title: Saranapala v. Solanga Arachchi, Senior Superintendent of Police and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 470/96 (FR), decided on 18 June 1997

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the prohibition of the NSSP May Day procession violated the petitioner's right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the police selectively prohibited the NSSP procession while allowing other political parties to hold processions and meetings, thus violating his right to equality and equal protection under the law.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the prohibition was based on security concerns and was a lawful exercise of police powers under section 77(3) of the Police Ordinance and emergency regulations, not discriminatory.
key_facts: The NSSP was initially granted permission for a May Day procession and meeting.
Permission was revoked citing security reasons shortly before May Day.
Other political parties, including the LSSP, were allowed to hold processions and meetings on the same day.
The NSSP procession was stopped by police, but a limited group led by Dr. Karunaratne was allowed to proceed.
The petitioner alleged discrimination based on political opinion.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and equal protection, requiring even-handed application of laws and regulations. The police failed to apply section 77(3) of the Police Ordinance and emergency regulations evenly, selectively prohibiting the NSSP procession while permitting others, thus violating the petitioner's right to equality.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found no credible security threat justifying the selective prohibition. Evidence showed other parties were allowed processions and meetings, indicating discriminatory treatment against the NSSP based on political opinion.
principles_established: Equal protection requires non-discriminatory and even-handed application of laws.
Selective enforcement of police powers against a political party violates Article 12(1).
Restrictions on fundamental rights must not be a pretext for suppressing free expression.
precedents_cited: Joseph Perera v. The Attorney-General (1992) 1 Sri LR 199, 214, 218

outcome.holding: The Court held that the respondents violated the petitioner's fundamental right to equality before the law and equal protection under Article 12(1) by selectively prohibiting the NSSP procession.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 15,000 as costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the Court's finding that the police failed to apply the law evenly and discriminated against the petitioner, violating his right to equal protection under the law.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: By permitting members of other political parties to march while denying or seriously abridging the petitioner’s right to march, the respondents failed to act even handedly in applying the provisions of section 77 (3) of the Police Ordinance and the Emergency Regulations and thereby violated the petitioner's fundamental right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law declared by Article 12 (1) of the Constitution.
